lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on reform in hard times
lead.head: Never waste a crisis? Fear one

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 123

body: India got some out­stand­ing re­forms done in 1991, in the mid­dle of an eco­nomic cri­sis. Ever since, Amit Varma said, peo­ple have par­roted the con­ven­tional wis­dom that you can only make great, sweep­ing changes in a cri­sis.
On Episode 123 of *Everything is Everything*, Varma and Ajay Shah set out to bust that myth.

The be­lief, Varma said, mis­takes cor­re­la­tion for cau­sa­tion. It also com­mits se­lec­tion bias, look­ing at one cri­sis that ended well and ig­nor­ing what crises in gen­eral can do, which can be quite dis­as­trous. {#correlation}
Shah put it more bluntly. “I ac­tu­ally want to say this up­side down that crises are truly dan­ger­ous times,” he said. {123-C01}
## The pol­icy pipe­line
A cri­sis, Shah ar­gued, can only help if the ideas and the peo­ple are al­ready in place, built up­stream of the pol­i­cy­mak­ers long be­fore. Otherwise it is fully wasted.

Varma, who once be­lieved 1991 hap­pened only be­cause India had no choice, found the real story through his own con­ver­sa­tions. From the late 1960s, Manmohan Singh had qui­etly built a com­mu­nity of thinkers. When the cri­sis came, Varma said, “ev­ery­thing was in place.” {123-S01}

Shah turned to the thinker John Kingdon, for whom change needs three streams to meet: a prob­lem, pol­icy ideas and the pol­i­tics. A cri­sis can bring the prob­lem and the pol­i­tics. The pol­icy has to be built in peace­time.

The 2012 Nirbhaya case showed what hap­pens oth­er­wise. The prob­lem and the pol­i­tics came to­gether, but no­body had spent twenty years on the ideas, and the mo­ment pro­duced only some ac­tivist-style law­mak­ing.
## In the wrong hands
Worse, a cri­sis can help the wrong peo­ple. The checks and bal­ances of so­ci­ety break down, Shah said, and in India, an early-stage democ­racy, they are weak to begin with.

The tem­plate, he said, comes from the philoso­pher Carl Schmitt: the true ruler is one who can sus­pend the rule of law in a cri­sis. Indira Gandhi’s Emergency of 1975 came after in­fla­tion of 16 per cent in 1974. Hitler used the Reichstag fire to sus­pend Germany’s con­sti­tu­tion.
Even with­out mal­ice, Shah said, a weak state with low ca­pa­bil­ity can make a cri­sis worse.
Hence his tax­on­omy. A cri­sis with­out pre­pared ideas is wasted. In a frag­ile state it in­vites au­thor­i­tar­i­ans. In a state of low ca­pa­bil­ity it brings a flood of in­co­her­ent mea­sures.
## Work in peace­time

So what should a re­former do? Not wait for a cri­sis, Shah said, and not en­gi­neer one, but make progress every day, with hu­mil­ity. “So fix the roof while the sun is shin­ing, build the com­mu­nity, build the peo­ple, chip away, be a brick­layer.” {123-C13}
Varma brought the ar­gu­ment home. A heart scare ear­lier this year, which left him with a stent, and di­a­betes be­fore it, both pushed him into re­forms of his own life­style.

But he could have died, he said, and he had al­ways known what a healthy life looked like. He lacked the dis­ci­pline to live it. Had India done the right things be­fore, the 1991 cri­sis would never have oc­curred.
The metaphor has a flaw, he ad­mit­ted. A per­son can re­spond to a cri­sis far more co­her­ently than a state, with all its stake­hold­ers and bad in­cen­tives.
“It is in peace times that you win the next war by mak­ing sure the next war doesn’t hap­pen,” Varma said. {123-S12}

second.label: The 1974 inflation
second.head: Eight going on economist
second.deck: At eight, Ajay Shah saw through Indira Gandhi’s blame game on prices

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Indira Gandhi’s hoarders

body: Ajay Shah used to watch Indira Gandhi blame the in­fla­tion of 1974 on hoard­ers and spec­u­la­tors, bad peo­ple hold­ing goods. He was eight that year, and he al­ready knew that prices are made by sup­ply and de­mand.

He was gen­uinely baf­fled. She had re­ceived “all those beau­ti­ful let­ters”, *Glimpses of World History*, so she must be a smart per­son. So why, he won­dered, was Indira Gandhi so clue­less? {123-J04}

Grown up, he un­der­stood. It was pop­ulism: stoke ha­tred against the elites, and no­body blames you for mess­ing up mon­e­tary pol­icy. {123-S09} That oth­er­ing, he said, be­came the full-blown *Garibi Hatao* ide­ol­ogy, and the at­tacks on privy purses.

quote.text: When I grew up, I un­der­stood this is pop­ulism. You want to stoke ha­tred against the elites.

third.head: 1,324 press releases later

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the flood of press releases

body: After de­mon­eti­sa­tion, Ajay Shah said, the RBI re­leased 74 reg­u­la­tions in 50 days. There had been no plan­ning, so it worked things out on the fly, and made a bad sit­u­a­tion worse. {#rbi}
During COVID, the Ministry of Health re­leased 1,324 press re­leases. “What sense does that make?” Shah asked. {123-S10}

To him this was what the econ­o­mist Lant Pritchett calls pre­ma­ture load bear­ing. An in­sti­tu­tion given more than it can carry does not rise to the task; it col­lapses into or­gan­i­sa­tional rout, and the re­sult is chaos.

The 2013 taper tantrum was an­other case. Ben Bernanke made some re­marks to a jour­nal­ist, mar­kets swung around the world, and the RBI and the Ministry of Finance, Shah said, turned a medium prob­lem into a much big­ger one.

from1.head: Never waste a crisis? Fear one

quote.text: Well, many ter­ri­ble ideas are also nor­mal­ized when you have a cri­sis and the Overton win­dow is widened.

box.title: A line before Game of Thrones
box.text: Ajay Shah first set out the idea that crises are lad­ders for the wrong peo­ple in *In Service of the Republic*, his book with Vijay Kelkar, which Amit Varma calls Shah’s “fine book”. {123-R01}

sections.label: The steelman
sections.head: In praise of disaster
sections.caption: the case for a crisis
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah to steel­man the view he would go on to at­tack. Shah began with a line he at­trib­uted to Rahm Emanuel, who he thought was Barack Obama’s chief of staff: a cri­sis is a ter­ri­ble thing to waste. {123-J09}

Behavioural psy­chol­ogy lends sup­port, he said. In prospect the­ory, peo­ple take the world around them as their base­line and, being loss-averse, do not want to rock the boat. In a cri­sis the world seems to be going to hell any­way, so peo­ple look at new things.

His ex­am­ple was food. Through the 1950s and 1960s, many peo­ple knew what needed fix­ing, but it was not get­ting done. Then the kharif crops of 1965 and 1966 failed, India came to the verge of mass star­va­tion, and the United States bailed it out with food grain. {123-S02}
That fo­cused minds. Indira Gandhi and C. Subramaniam pushed high-yielding va­ri­eties, fer­tilis­ers and ir­ri­ga­tion, and India got the Green Revolution.
## The Overton win­dow
But a cri­sis widens the Overton win­dow, the range of ideas the pub­lic will ac­cept, in both di­rec­tions, Shah warned. Terrible ideas are nor­malised too.

~ Varma has pushed two win­dows him­self. On free­dom, as a tar­iff and free speech ab­so­lutist, the game is long. On pod­cast length he claims vic­tory: after his ten-hour and twelve-hour episodes, an hour is no longer a deep dive. {123-S11}

quote.text: Well, many ter­ri­ble ideas are also nor­mal­ized when you have a cri­sis and the Overton win­dow is widened.

sections.label: The prerequisites
sections.head: Upstream of the policymaker
sections.caption: the policy pipeline
body: Before ac­tion, Ajay Shah said, ideas and peo­ple have to be in place, or a cri­sis is fully wasted.

Helping a pol­i­cy­maker im­ple­ment what they al­ready want is a noble im­pulse, he said, but not of essence. Implement ev­ery­thing that a thou­sand good Indian pol­i­cy­mak­ers want today, and he doubted it would make India much bet­ter. {123-C03}

Fresh think­ing comes from out­side. Shah re­called a sto­ried eco­nom­ics bu­reau­crat, very good to him per­son­ally, who in the run-up to 1991 was “stub­bornly un­able to see that this is bro­ken”, de­fend­ing his own legacy. {123-S03}
## Activism and wonkery

After Nirbhaya, Shah wrote a blog post, *Activism and wonkery are the yin and yang*. {123-R11} Shouting on the streets helps, he said, but real sys­tems have many mov­ing parts, and some­one must have sim­u­lated them in their mind.
Social media, he added, has pro­duced many more ac­tivists, but not more of those peo­ple.

~ It takes pa­tience. Shah, Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi fin­ished the first fully worked-out GST pro­posal in 2003; the first move to­wards a com­plete GST came in 2016. “It takes five hun­dred sem­i­nars and con­fer­ences to argue about the GST,” he said. {123-S05}

quote.text: If you don’t have all that wonkery, then all the ac­tivism of the world is point­less.

sections.label: Chaos is a ladder
sections.head: The true ruler’s moment
sections.caption: Carl Schmitt’s true ruler
body: Ajay Shah wrote “chaos is a lad­der” in *In Service of the Republic*, his book with Vijay Kelkar, Amit Varma said, only to find the line was also in *Game of Thrones*. {123-J03}

In a cri­sis, Shah said, the norms that re­strain power stop work­ing, and a cer­tain kind of pol­icy en­tre­pre­neur uses the mad­ness to do very bad things. India, he noted, is only 80 years old as a democ­racy. {#democracy}
He cited Carl Schmitt, a philoso­pher who played a role in the emer­gence of the Nazis, for whom the true ruler is one who can sus­pend the rule of law in a cri­sis.
## From in­fla­tion to Emergency
Shah traced the 1975 Emergency back to the 1971 war, an enor­mous fis­cal prob­lem, and to 1974, when in­fla­tion reached 16 per cent. “Inflation tears the so­ci­ety apart,” he said. {123-C08}
The JP Narayan move­ment fol­lowed, buses were burned, and Indira Gandhi, a “true ruler”, sus­pended the rule of law. {123-S06}
In Germany, a hy­per­in­fla­tion after the First World War came first, and Hitler later used the Reichstag fire to sus­pend the con­sti­tu­tion.
~ Monetary econ­o­mists, Shah said, should be held re­spon­si­ble for such dis­as­ters, as for the good done since in­fla­tion tar­get­ing. Varma added the bad lead­ers who over­rule them.

quote.text: Indira Gandhi was a true ruler. Who sus­pended rule of law in that time of cri­sis.

sections.label: Weak states
sections.head: Malice, or just muddle?
sections.caption: malice and incompetence
body: Amit Varma told Ajay Shah he loved his beard, then of­fered him a razor: Hanlon’s. Never at­tribute to mal­ice, it says, what can be ad­e­quately ex­plained by stu­pid­ity. {123-J06}

Malice, Shah said, does the most harm where checks and bal­ances are weak. Hitler de­stroyed the Weimar Republic, an early-stage democ­racy still fig­ur­ing out the ba­sics. The United States, a bet­ter democ­racy, saw more lim­ited depre­da­tions after 9/11.

He told a story from Jim Comey, then at the top of the US na­tional se­cu­rity es­tab­lish­ment, who rushed by car to a hos­pi­tal to brief a des­per­ately ill of­fi­cial be­fore some­thing bad was done about a mass sur­veil­lance pro­gramme. {123-S08}
In a fledg­ling democ­racy, Shah said, most of us would just bow our heads and go along.
## Giants and pyg­mies
Then there is in­com­pe­tence. “Government is the power of gi­ants given to pyg­mies who are try­ing to re­spond on a day to day basis on a cri­sis,” Shah said. {123-C09}

~ On de­mon­eti­sa­tion, Shah said a more ca­pa­ble state would have planned it bet­ter, though he did not sup­port it. Varma went fur­ther: “A more com­pe­tent state would never have done some­thing so daft and id­i­otic as de­mon­eti­sa­tion.”

quote.text: You need those peo­ple, you need those amaz­ing peo­ple who will stand up and fight for the rule of law

sections.label: Incrementalism
sections.head: No French Revolutions, please
sections.caption: Popper and the British way
body: A good coun­try, Ajay Shah said, makes progress every day, and that progress comes from in­cre­men­tal­ism: thinkers crit­i­cise the sta­tus quo, their ideas be­come main­stream and slowly per­co­late to pol­i­cy­mak­ers.

He drew on the philoso­pher Karl Popper, who sep­a­rated utopian from in­cre­men­tal so­cial en­gi­neer­ing. Grand schemes, like col­lec­tivis­ing all the farms of the USSR, gen­er­ally lead to a ter­ri­ble mess. {123-C11}
“Sad is a coun­try that needs a hero. Sad is a coun­try that needs a cri­sis,” he said. {#sad}
## Britain against France

The French Revolution tore so­ci­ety down, Shah said, and set France back for many years. Britain left monar­chy for lib­eral democ­racy in­cre­men­tally. Its one crit­i­cal mile­stone came when Republicans led by Cromwell cut off the head of Charles I; Parliament’s power grew grad­u­ally, and Britain be­came the most suc­cess­ful coun­try in the world.

Closer to home, he lived through the re­form of India’s eq­uity mar­ket from 1992 till about 2007, a col­lab­o­ra­tion of the fi­nance min­istry, SEBI, NSE and aca­demics, driven by data and re­search. {#equity}
~ Both hosts call them­selves con­ser­va­tive in Edmund Burke’s sense: not against change, but hum­ble about a com­plex world in which every step has un­in­tended con­se­quences. {123-C12}

quote.text: I think both of us are lib­eral in our ends, con­ser­va­tive in our means.

sections.label: The lessons
sections.head: Bricklayers, not saviours
sections.caption: how crises go wrong
body: Ajay Shah ended with a rough tax­on­omy. Without pre­pared ideas, a cri­sis is use­less. In a frag­ile state, would-be au­to­crats de­clare them­selves the true ruler. In a state with low ca­pa­bil­ity, the re­sult is “a hun­dred in­co­her­ent pol­icy mea­sures”.

Coherence, he said, means un­der­stand­ing the world and find­ing one strat­egy for dis­parate prob­lems. Practical peo­ple, solv­ing each prob­lem ex­pe­di­ently, pro­duce ac­tions that make a mess with each other. {123-C10}
## Humble, twice

The reformer’s job is to work in peace­time, Shah said: not to wait for a cri­sis or en­gi­neer one, but to lay one brick at a time. He asked for hu­mil­ity twice, be­cause none of us knows the world, and be­cause we must admit when the ev­i­dence shows we were wrong. {123-C13}

Amit Varma said his own heart scare and di­a­betes came be­cause he lacked the dis­ci­pline for a healthy life he knew about. But a per­son re­sponds to a cri­sis far bet­ter than a state, with its mov­ing parts and stake­hold­ers.

~ Shah closed by read­ing Max Weber: pol­i­tics is a strong and slow bor­ing of hard boards, and those who are nei­ther lead­ers nor he­roes must arm them­selves with stead­fast­ness of heart. {#weber}

quote.text: Coherence is an intellectual’s word. It is a philosopher’s word.
The prob­lems are up­stream. You need to change the ideas, you need to change the imag­i­na­tion, you need to build a cadre of peo­ple who are up­stream of the pol­i­cy­mak­ers

p3.title: Tales from the brink
p3.deck: A long relay, a wasted outrage, laws in a rush and a heart scare

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the people who prepared India’s 1991 reforms
stories.head: The baton was passed long before
body: Amit Varma used to think the 1991 re­forms came about only be­cause of the bal­ance of pay­ments cri­sis: in that mo­ment the gov­ern­ment had no choice but to re­form, though it did not re­ally want to.

Several episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen* and *Everything is Everything* changed his mind. The story, he found, started much ear­lier, and in that long arc Manmohan Singh is an even greater hero than one would think.

From the late 1960s, Singh was build­ing a com­mu­nity in silent ways. He asked Vijay Kelkar to come back to India in the early 1970s, and Montek Singh Ahluwalia in the late 1970s. It was not ex­actly an or­gan­ised ef­fort, Varma said, but it peo­pled the ecosys­tem with in­ter­est­ing thinkers.

From the late 1970s, as Ahluwalia de­scribed in his con­ver­sa­tion with Varma, a bunch of peo­ple, many of them in­side gov­ern­ment, thought qui­etly about how to make India bet­ter. They picked their bat­tles, and did not fight los­ing ones that could cost them their place.
In 1990, Varma said, Ahluwalia came out with the fa­mous M doc­u­ment, “a work of leg­end”, which con­tained much of what was done a year later. {#mdoc}
“So when the ninety one cri­sis hap­pened, ev­ery­thing was in place,” he said. Nobody was floun­der­ing; the body of work was there. {123-S01}

~ Ajay Shah com­pared it to a relay. We see the last ten sec­onds of the run­ner car­ry­ing the baton across the line and think, wow, you did it. But the baton had passed through many ear­lier stages of the pol­icy pipe­line.
stories.why: A cri­sis can open a win­dow, but it can­not fill it. In 1991 the prob­lem and the pol­i­tics met a pol­icy stream that pa­tient peo­ple had spent fif­teen or twenty years pre­par­ing. {123-C04}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the long road to 1991

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on what came of public outrage in 2012
stories.head: Outrage without a blueprint
body: In 2012, the hor­rific Nirbhaya rape case in Delhi brought the prob­lem and the pol­i­tics to­gether, two of the three streams in John Kingdon’s frame­work, Ajay Shah said. Manmohan Singh and Montek Singh Ahluwalia wanted to use the mo­ment to re­form the crim­i­nal jus­tice sys­tem.

But the pol­icy leg was not ready. Nobody had spent twenty years build­ing peo­ple, doc­u­ments, books, sem­i­nars and con­fer­ences, and an in­ter­con­nected pic­ture of how the parts fit to­gether. “None of this can be hatched in a hurry,” Shah said.
“A cri­sis is a ter­ri­ble thing to waste, and the Nirbhaya cri­sis was wasted,” he said. It pro­duced only some ac­tivist-style law­mak­ing, which did not move the nee­dle. {123-S04}
~ Shah had told the story be­fore, in the hosts’ episode *The Long Road to Change*.
stories.why: Public out­rage and po­lit­i­cal will are not enough. If no­body has worked out the ideas in calm times, the win­dow closes with noth­ing to show for it. Activism, Shah ar­gued, needs wonkery. {123-C05}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the wasted Nirbhaya moment

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the laws that rode in after 9/11
stories.head: Whoosh, and it was law
body: For a long time, Ajay Shah said, a hawk­ish part of the United States na­tional se­cu­rity es­tab­lish­ment had been nurs­ing au­thor­i­tar­ian ideas: the Patriot Act, coun­ter­ing the fi­nanc­ing of ter­ror, anti-money laun­der­ing and the FATF, which in India means the Prevention of Money Laundering Act and the Enforcement Directorate.
In nor­mal times, he said, prin­ci­pled law­mak­ers in the Senate and the House of Representatives would have de­bated such things and re­fused them as au­thor­i­tar­i­an­ism.
“And then came the 9/11 at­tacks and like whoosh, within weeks all this stuff got through,” Shah said. {123-S07}
~ By and large, he said, every piece was a bad idea. Tracing money flows has never dis­rupted a ter­ror­ist plot; all it has done is build a mass sur­veil­lance sys­tem in fi­nance.
stories.why: This is the 1991 story with the sign flipped. Bad ideas can also wait in the pipe­line, and a cri­sis lets them through as read­ily as good ones: ter­ri­ble ideas, too, are nor­malised. {123-C02}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the 9/11 wish list

stories.kicker: Amit Varma takes the argument to his own health
stories.head: The patient who knew the cure
body: Earlier this year Amit Varma had a heart scare and got a stent. Before that came di­a­betes, which he re­versed through diet. Both crises pushed him into re­forms of his own.

He could have died, he said, and he had al­ways known what a healthy life looked like. He lacked the dis­ci­pline to ex­er­cise every day, do re­sis­tance train­ing, avoid sugar and sleep prop­erly. Had he lived that way, nei­ther cri­sis would have come.

Countries are the same: had India done the right things be­fore 1991, that cri­sis would never have oc­curred. “It is in peace times that you win the next war by mak­ing sure the next war doesn’t hap­pen,” he said. {123-S12}
~ But the metaphor is flawed, he said. A per­son re­sponds to a cri­sis far more co­her­ently than a state, full of stake­hold­ers and bad in­cen­tives.

quote.text: A cri­sis is not to be wished.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah found the anal­ogy re­mark­able, and hoped we can all turn a per­sonal cri­sis into a mo­ment of rein­ven­tion. {#analogy}

quiz.q: Which two harvests failed back to back, bringing India close to mass starvation?
quiz.a: The kharif crops of 1965 and 1966; the United States sent food grain.

quiz.q: According to John Kingdon, which three streams must come together for meaningful change?
quiz.a: A prob­lem stream, a pol­icy stream and a pol­i­tics stream, all at once.

quiz.q: Who, by Amit Varma’s account, came out with the famous M document in 1990?
quiz.a: Montek Singh Ahluwalia; it held much of the re­form done a year later.

quiz.q: What, by Ajay Shah’s account, did Carl Schmitt say marks the true ruler?
quiz.a: The abil­ity to sus­pend the rule of law in a time of cri­sis.

quiz.q: How many years passed between the first worked-out GST proposal and the first real move?
quiz.a: Thirteen: the re­port was done in 2003, and the move came in 2016.

quiz.q: Whose razor did Amit Varma hand Ajay Shah, and what does it say?
quiz.a: Hanlon’s: never at­tribute to mal­ice what can be ad­e­quately ex­plained by stu­pid­ity.

The pop­ulist ide­ol­ogy that grew from oth­er­ing the elites, per Shah

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 123. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Max Weber (Ernst Gottmann, public domain); James Comey (Federal Bureau of Investigation, public domain).

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Episode 285 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s first-hand ac­count of his decades in the re­form en­gine room and the ‘silent revolution’ that built up from the late 1970s.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: The 1991 Project
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan’s trea­sure trove of chron­i­cles and oral his­to­ries of the 1991 re­forms, in­clud­ing the leg­endary ‘M document’.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on labels
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite episodes: what la­bels like lib­eral and con­ser­va­tive re­ally mean, why na­tion­al­ism dif­fers from pa­tri­o­tism, and the hosts’ own con­ser­vatism of chang­ing the world care­fully, one step at a time, be­cause of un­in­tended con­se­quences.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Everything is Everything episode)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on KYC
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case that India’s KYC regime has mainly built mass sur­veil­lance of citizens’ fi­nances while never stop­ping a ter­ror­ist plot, and that the real dan­ger is a state watch­ing cit­i­zens and turn­ing its co­er­cive power on them.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on populism
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Populism is not ‘what is popular’ but a dan­ger­ous pack­age of be­liefs and meth­ods, ris­ing world­wide along­side na­tion­al­ism, that works by in­vent­ing en­e­mies and sell­ing in­su­lar slo­gans like im­port sub­sti­tu­tion.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on reversing diabetes
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: Activism and wonkery are the yin and yang
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ar­gues that street and so­cial-media ac­tivism is use­ful but use­less with­out care­ful con­cep­tual work about how a com­plex sys­tem ac­tu­ally fits to­gether.

shelf.title: XKDR Forum
shelf.why: Ajay’s re­search or­gan­i­sa­tion, which builds a body of work in areas like law and eco­nom­ics so that the pol­icy ideas are ready when the prob­lem and the pol­i­tics line up; its work­ing pa­pers and YouTube chan­nel are where he points peo­ple who ask him to teach.

shelf.title: The LEAP Blog
shelf.why: The peer-reviewed re­search blog Ajay co-edits, where his ideas are avail­able to any­one at any time.

laughs.text: Ajay asks who was key on the IMF side of the 1991 pro­gram. Amit an­swers Urjit Patel (‘See, my GK is in place’) and then men­tions A.N. Varma, ‘not re­lated to me’, who was also crit­i­cal: ‘So you get good things done with Varmas in the mix.’

Amit says Ajay wrote ‘Chaos is a ladder’ in In Service of the Republic on his own, only to find out later it is also in Game of Thrones. Amit voices Ajay’s dis­ap­point­ment: ‘it’s such a great line I came up with it, but you know, if shit hap­pens, man.’

Amit checks that Ajay’s eighth birth­day was 7 August 1974, the year of record in­fla­tion. Ajay: ‘So I was like fully in the know by that time. Like sup­ply and de­mand was some­thing, you know, that every child knew. So why was Indira Gandhi so clue­less?’
Amit in­tro­duces Hanlon’s razor: ‘Ajay, I love your beard, but I want to give to you a razor.’

Rain stops the out­door record­ing. Ajay vows to carry on ‘with­out an or­gan­i­sa­tional rout’, a call­back to Lant Pritchett. Indoors, Amit says ‘as our good friend Obelix would say, the sky fell on our heads.’ He men­tions his com­fort bear Freddy, named after Bastiat and Hayek, is re­lieved Ajay ‘did not throw a tantrum’, and uses that to segue into the 2013 taper tantrum.
‘A cri­sis is a ter­ri­ble thing to waste’ is at­trib­uted to Rahm Emanuel, Barack Obama’s chief of staff. Ajay notes it plays on ‘the mind is a ter­ri­ble thing to waste.’
The Reichstag fire, which Hitler used to mo­nop­o­lise power and sus­pend the con­sti­tu­tion, is Ajay’s prime ex­am­ple of a cri­sis seized by a ‘true ruler’.

Max Weber, read at the close: ‘Politics is a strong and slow bor­ing of hard boards. It takes both pas­sion and per­spec­tive… even those who are nei­ther lead­ers nor he­roes must arm them­selves with that stead­fast­ness of heart which can brave even the crum­bling of all hopes.’
